title: Why Are Europe’s Small Central Banks Stocking Up Foreign Money?
text:
ZURICH—Europe’s smaller central banks are loading up on foreign currencies at rates usually associated with periods of intense global stress, highlighting the fragile underpinnings of the global economic recovery despite the recent upbeat mood in financial markets.

Switzerland’s holdings of foreign assets jumped last month at their fastest pace in over two years as its central bank fought the strong franc, which weakens exports and inflation. The Czech central bankintervened in January on a massive scale to maintain its currency target against the euro. Denmark has also stepped up its foreign-currency purchases to keep the krone from strengthening too much.

These central banks are showing crisis-like behavior to protect their currencies even in the absence of obvious trouble. This exposes them to losses if their currencies fail to weaken on their own. It also raises doubts as to how long they can keep this up in an era when economic and political uncertainties appear to be a lasting feature of the world economy.

“There is a little bit of survivor behavior,” said Peter Rosenstreich, head of market strategy at Swissquote Bank. “They’ve been protecting their currencies so long and it’s hard to give up that defensive position.”

The Swiss National Bank said Tuesday its foreign exchange reserves swelled nearly 25 billion Swiss francs ($24.63 billion) last month to 668 billion francs, the biggest rise since December 2014, the month before the Swiss abandoned a cap on the franc’s value. The pile of foreign reserves is greater than Switzerland’s entire gross domestic product.

“It’s quite bizarre. You’d think at some time you’d run out of surprises,” said Stefan Gerlach, chief economist at BSI Bank in Zurich and a former deputy governor at Ireland’s central bank.

The franc is regarded as one of the world’s safest currencies given Switzerland’s stable economy and low debt, meaning its value usually increases when investors seek safety instead of returns.

Analysts cited elections in France this spring, in Germany this fall and continued political uncertainty in Italy, the U.S. and U.K. as reasons for the relentless demand for the franc and other safe-haven currencies.

Central banks accumulate foreign reserves when they purchase assets denominated in other currencies, using freshly created money. They do this to weaken their currencies, protecting exports and giving a boost to inflation. Foreign reserves can waver slightly due to changes in currency values, but big increases like Switzerland’s signal aggressive intervention.

This tool has gained traction in recent years as official rates have turned negative in Denmark and Switzerland and are near zero in the Czech Republic.

The Czech central bank said Tuesday that currency intervention was 14.5 billion euros ($15.3 billion) in January, the largest amount by far since it introduced an exchange rate target against the euro in November 2013. “It is an eye-popping number,” said Bruna Skarica, economist at Oxford Economics.

Czech officials have said they plan to discontinue this target in the middle of this year, which has spurred investor flows into the Czech currency, the koruna, in anticipation.

Denmark intervened last month to the tune of 4.7 billion kroner ($670 million), the most since last June.

Like the franc, the Danish krone typically rises in uncertain times, especially in the eurozone. The Czech Republic is seen as one of the more stable economies within central and Eastern Europe, so it sees similar trends.

What sets this latest episode apart is that there wasn’t a particular destabilizing stress point in the last few weeks like the Greek crisis or the U.K. vote to leave the European Union. Global markets have been mostly calm with U.S. equities marking record highs. Government bond yields have risen but not too much.

Meanwhile, the U.S. Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank are close to hitting their 2% inflation targets, and the Fed is expected to raise interest rates as soon as next week.

This should be a recipe for reduced demand for the Swiss, Danish and Czech currencies as investors seek higher returns elsewhere. But the opposite has occurred.

The euro traded at 1.0723 francs midday Tuesday, about 10% lower than it was when the SNB had the franc ceiling in place from 2011 to early 2015. The euro fetched 7.43 Danish kroner, which is within the Danish bank’s target of within 2.25% above or below 7.46. The Czech koruna is near the central bank’s target of 27 against the euro, but only due to the massive intervention.

“The global economy is doing better than in the last few years” and has broadened out, SNB Chairman Thomas Jordan said in a Swiss newspaper interview on March 4.

But alluding to the contrast between a better economy and heightened political tension that has bedeviled his central bank, Mr. Jordan noted the political risks are on the rise.

“Such phases of increased political uncertainty are problematic for us because the Swiss franc is considered a safe haven,” he said.

An earlier version of this article incorrectly stated the amount of the intervention. (March 7)

title: UPDATE 1-Czech c.banker says need to see inflation above target to exit  FX  policy
text:
(Adds quotes, estimated volume of interventions)

PRAGUE, Sept 15 (Reuters) - The Czech Republic's central bank needs to see inflation overshooting its 2 percent target in its policy forecasts before it considers exiting its weak crown policy, board member Jiri Rusnok was quoted as saying on Tuesday.

The central bank has pledged to keep the crown on the weak side of around 27 to the euro until at least the second half of 2016 to spur price growth.

Rusnok said the timing of the exit depended on future forecasts and reiterated the bank never ruled out delaying it.

"The forecasts quite evolve, although the moves are small, by tenths (of percentage points)," he said in an interview with Hospodarske Noviny due to be published on Wednesday.

"We have to take it seriously. We never ruled out we could exit the interventions later. We have always said 'minimum' or 'at least'."

The bank has forecast inflation, which slowed to an annual rate of 0.3 percent in August, reaching its target only in early 2017. Asked about the chances of an exit in 2017, Rusnok said it would rely on future forecasts.

"It will be key for us to see a clear reaching, but I would say overshooting, of the inflation target in the horizon of 12 to 18 months," Rusnok said.

"Inflation should head above 2 percent, that means between 2 and 3 percent."

After launching the policy in 2013, the central bank has only now had to intervene to keep the crown at bay after it firmed this year thanks to an accelerating economy whose pace is among the fastest in the European Union.

The bank first intervened in mid-July. Data released last week showed it bought 1 billion euros that month.

Analysts estimate it tripled that amount in August and has accelerated the tactic even more this month. ING estimated the central bank printed 60 billion crowns (2.22 billion euros) in early September.

Rusnok echoed remarks by Governor Miroslav Singer - who will be replaced by Rusnok next July - that the central bank did not have to worry about its reserves.

"Should we get somewhere around the half of GDP, that would still be reserves of an acceptable level for a country of our type," he said.

"I don't see anything wrong with having very decent foreign exchange reserves."

Rusnok said that the pressure for more monetary easing was less than half a year ago but said he could not rule out the option of negative interest rates if they were needed. (Reporting by Robert Muller and Jason Hovet; Editing by Hugh Lawson and Jonathan Oatis)

title: CEE Morning Briefing: Hungary  Central Bank  in Focus
text:
TODAY'S CALENDAR 
Local/GMT 
1400/1200 Hungary central 
          bank rate call 
1500/1300 Hungary central 
          bank statement 
 

Hungary is widely expected to continue its easing cycle on Tuesday as its currency has weathered the financial market storm caused by the Greek crisis relatively well.

"Things have turned slightly worse but remain at very supportive levels. Put simply, we think the Hungarian central bank cares that Hungary is not standing out in risk-terms versus peers, especially as it moves to cut [interest rates] below [those of regional peer] Poland," said Nonumar economist Peter Attard Montalto.

Poland's benchmark monetary policy rate is at 1.5%, the same as Hungary's key rate. But both are still above the Czech Republic's headline rate of 0.05% and near-zero interest rates in the euro area, the main trading partner for all economies in Central Europe.

Hungary is set to cut its main rate to a fresh record low, albeit at a slower pace than in each of the previous three months, 15 of the 17 economists polled said. Most of them forecast a 0.10 percentage-point easing this time around, compared with the 0.15-percentage-point moves in each of the previous three months.

The Hungarian easing cycle is predicted to bottom out at either 1.2% or 1.3%.

title: Czech  Central Bank  Willing to Resume  Forex Intervention
text:
PRAGUE--The European Central Bank's latest measures to combat eurozone deflation are taking their toll on the Czech Republic, whose central bank Thursday warned that it may intervene again to keep the koruna weak against the euro.

The Czech central bank also extended the duration of keeping the koruna weak from the previously stated exit date of early 2016 until at least the second half of next year, and possibly for the duration of the year.

The weakening euro and falling oil prices are creating "unusually high levels of uncertainty" and adding fresh downward pressure to Czech prices, central bank Governor Miroslav Singer said, adding that as a result the bank expects deflation later this year.

That is a cold shower for the bank which was forced to devalue the koruna in late 2013 after earlier setting its interest rates at near zero levels.

In November 2013, the Czech central bank spent more than EUR7 billion in a one-day assault on markets that weakened the koruna more than 5% against the euro, staved off domestic deflation, and pulled the country out of a two-year long recession. The central bank said at the time it wouldn't allow the koruna to firm beyond 27 against the euro.

The Czech central bank's benchmark interest rate is 0.05%, making it the loosest monetary policy east of the eurozone. The monetary policy board says it won't move into negative interest rates.

So with deflation looming, the only primary tool left to further ease monetary conditions is another devaluation. Mr. Singer is ready to act if needed.

"The central bank is prepared to move the exchange rate commitment to a weaker level if there were to be a long-term increase in deflationary pressures capable of causing a slump in domestic demand, renewed risks of deflation in the Czech economy and a systematic decrease in inflation expectations," Mr. Singer said.

Unlike in most countries in central Europe, Czech inflation was accelerating for most of 2014. But as of late, consumer price growth has stagnated and deflationary tendencies are looming largely due to the euro's weakness. Since the central bank's 2013 intervention, the euro has lost over 15% to the dollar.

On Thursday afternoon the koruna was trading steadily at 27.72 to the euro. Some analysts say the currency is too strong at current levels and barring another devaluation, prices are bound to decline.

William Jackson, analyst at Capital Economics in London, said it is looking increasingly likely that Czechs will weaken the koruna, and he suggested 29 to the euro as an estimate.

Mr. Singer said it is impossible to predict where the central bank will set a new ceiling, saying the scope of such a policy step would be determined later by market sentiment, market interest rates and other macroeconomic factors.

The Czech central bank has an inflation target of 2% and on Thursday said it now expects consumer price growth of 1.1% in the first quarter of next year and 1.6% in the second quarter. The bank previously forecast inflation at 2.1% and 2.3%, respectively.

Negative spillover from the ECB's quantitative easing policy is also being felt in Denmark, where the central bank Thursday cut its deposit rate for the fourth time in less than three weeks. It has also intervened multiple times on the foreign-exchange market to prevent the krone from appreciating to what would be painful levels for the economy.

title: Macro Horizons: Welcome Signs of Easing in Eurozone, Doubts On China
text:
By Michael J. Casey and Alen Mattich

Macro Horizons covers the main macroeconomic and policy news events affecting foreign-exchange, fixed income and equity markets around the world, as selected by editors in New York, London and Hong Kong.

WRAP: Markets have received some rare upbeat news out of the Eurozone, where the ferocious credit squeeze seems to be relenting. With new European Central Bank liquidity measures coming in and its president, Mario Draghi, promising more if necessary, all while the euro is weakening, the momentum in monetary conditions could for the first time in years be headed in a more constructive direction to promote badly needed growth. Offsetting that positive news: the direction of monetary policy out of China could be thrown in doubt if Chinese leaders seeking to oust reform-minded governor of the People's Bank of China, Zhou Xiaochuan, have their way. Investors are figuring how to play that news, reported exclusively by The Wall Street Journal: do they buy on the short-term expectation that Mr. Zhou's departure would signal easier policy, or sell on the grounds that a reformer is being pushed aside and the longer-term risk to sustainable economic growth will be exacerbated. (AM, MC)

EUROZONE: The credit squeeze is easing.

--August M3 rose 2.0% on the year against a forecast rise of 1.9%.

--August private sector lending fell 1.5% from 1.6% in July.

Could it really be that the eurozone's credit squeeze is starting to ease? The pace at which private sector lending is falling has slowed, with lending to households picking up, even if business credit continues to contract. Meanwhile, the pace of money supply growth continues to pick up. Once the European Central Bank's recent policy provisions kick in, they should boost credit and money supply further still. (AM)

CHINA: Chinese leaders are discussing replacing Zhou Xiaochuan, the governor of the People's Bank of China, our Beijing bureau reported. The move reflects disagreements within the government over the financial reform agenda and concerns that Mr. Zhou's push for those reforms might stymie growth.

Domestic stock markets celebrated this news, the assumption being that it would usher in looser monetary policy, but if the change goes through, the long-term signal to foreign investors could be very bad indeed. Mr. Zhou has been the voice of reform, pushing for badly needed changes to the Chinese financial system--including interest rate liberalization and an open capital account. Without those reforms, it's hard to see how the Chinese economy can break free of an unsustainable model of growth in which artificially cheap bank loans finance relentless investment and construction without building up the consumer base. If Mr. Zhou's reform agenda is abandoned, it might ensure that there's more growth in the short term as that model is allowed to run a little longer, but the eventual downturn could be all the more painful when the investment bubble bursts. (MC)

TAIWAN: The central bank left its benchmark interest rates unchanged as expected, but signaled that tighter monetary policy could be on the horizon, with the governor, Perng Fai-nan, later saying that the monetary policy "tone" is switching to "neutral" from "accommodative."

Taiwanese rates haven't budged since July 2011, so the mere signal of a change is significant news. It reflects the surprising pickup that the local economy has undergone in recent months as demand for its all-important microchip and electronic components exports has surged. (MC)

AUSTRALIA: The Reserve Bank of Australia's governor, Glenn Stevens, said so-called macroprudential tools could prove useful in dousing the hot housing market, although he retained some doubts about their effectiveness .

Mr. Stevens's comments follow an RBA report Wednesday that it is talking to Australia Prudential Regulation Authority, or APRA, about containing mortgage lending. The RBA is trying to walk a tightrope between cooling the housing market on the one hand and keeping liquidity supplied to the otherwise weak broader economy on the other. (MC)

TURKEY: The Central Bank of Turkey kept its one-week repo interest rate at 8.25% and all other benchmark rates unchanged.

The decision could be seen as something of a compromise for Turkey's central bank. It is under pressure to cut rates from the government to boost jobs, with the unemployment rate up at an unhealthy 9.9%, but the economy is also facing inflation at 9.54%, well above the central bank's target of 5%, which would normally demand a rate hike. The decision reflects a political bind, in other words, perpetuating a difficult situation that will keep investors wary of buying the Turkish lira. (MC)

CZECH REPUBLIC: The Czech National Bank kept its benchmark rate at 0.05% and made no change to its foreign exchange intervention policy to weaken the koruna.

With the ECB now adopting fresh stimulus and the euro falling again, it's little surprise the Czech central bank took the decision to continue with monetary accommodation and currency intervention. The Czech Republic's economic circumstances are about as stark a contrast as you get from Turkey's. In fact, it's in a similar situation as Switzerland. The Czech economy has low inflation and is potentially at risk of deflation. Its central bank has set ultra-low interest rates but, like Switzerland's, has also been forced to adopt a currency intervention program to prevent the koruna from advancing above a fixed threshold euro. The Czech Republic has a healthy banking industry, also like Switzerland, but an export sector that's hurting from the eurozone's slowdown.

COMING UP:

U.S.: 8:30 a.m. EDT.

--August advancer report on durable goods. [Expected -17.5% vs. +22.6% in July.]

Don't be alarmed by those gigantic swings in the forecast. July's headline number was wildly distorted by some big aircraft sales for Boeing, and now economists expect payback in August. In fact, if you look at the ex-transportation number from last month's report it was down -0.8%, so that adjusted figure may even head in the other direction.

--Unemployment insurance weekly claims report. [Initial Claims expected 296,000 vs. 280,000 in prior week.]

After a couple of weeks in which the claims data had backed up a bit, we headed sharply lower again last week, re-affirming the impression that the labor market is truly now sustaining far fewer layoffs underway. This number at least--if not wages--reflects tighter labor conditions. It's one of those data points that helps build the hawk's case for a rate hike sooner rather than later.

U.S.: Time N/A. Federal Reserve Bank of AtlantaDennis Lockhart's speech at the U.S. Senator Thad Cochran Forum on American Enterprise.

Mr. Lockhart is this year a non-voter on the FOMC but is seen as an important moderate voice on the committee. So comments of his recently in which he was clearly reluctant to declare victory in the U.S. economic recovery and thus to consider a rate hike soon in the New Year were an important indication of the barriers to monetary tightening within the FOMC.

JAPAN: 7:30 p.m. EDT. (8:30 a.m. Friday, Tokyo)

--August national consumer prices index. [Core CPI was +3.3% on-year, overall CPI was +3.4% on-year, unchanged on month.]

--September CPI for Tokyo. [Core CPI was +2.7% on-year, overall CPI was +2.8% on-year, +0.2% on month.]

In the national CPI data for Japan you need to look at the monthly data. The headline annual numbers are distorted by the impact of the one-off sales tax increase in April, but in the monthly numbers we see, once again, an inclination toward disinflation. The good news is that Tokyo's data look a bit more reasonable and these lead the rest of the nation, since they come out a month earlier. Still, if there is no clear sign of the return to inflation sought by the central bank, the Bank of Japan may have to act. Markets will feel more convinced of that following comments from Governor Haruhiko Kuroda last week, who vowed to do what's necessary to achieve the BOJ's 2% annual inflation target (free of sales-tax-hike effects.)

text:
HRADEC KRALOVE, Czech Republic, Sept 9 (Reuters) - Exit from the Czech central bank's mode of keeping the crown currency's exchange rate weak will be smooth and the central bank can act easily on the market to help avoid any big fluctuations, Governor Miroslav Singer said on Tuesday.

The bank has kept a lid on the exchange rate since intervening to weaken the crown last November, pledging to intervene again if the currency firms below around 27 to the euro as part of its monetary policy easing, and plans to maintain that policy until 2016.

"I believe the exit will be relatively smooth, if not, then it is easy to solve, as everybody already knows," Singer said.

Exit should not bring any big jumps in part because traders do not have enough room to build big speculative positions due to tougher regulation, he said at a debate with businessmen. (Reporting by Robert Muller, writing by Jan Lopatka)

title: WRAPUP 1-Central European factory activity slows, Poland nears stagnation
text:
(Combines stories, adds quotes, details)

* Polish manufacturing PMI at 12-mth low of 50.3

* Czech PMI down to 54.7, below fcast, but still solid

* Data reflect divergence of Czech, Polish monetary policies

* Hungary's PMI falls to 51.5

By Marcin Goettig

WARSAW, July 1 (Reuters) - Factory activity slowed across central and eastern Europe in June, with Poland nearly in stagnation and the pace in the Czech Republic declining, although the latter is still growing and is cushioned by the country's ultra-loose monetary stance.

The manufacturing PMI index for Poland fell to a lower-than-expected 50.3 points last month, a 12-month low, from 50.8 in May, data compiled by Markit and HSBC showed.

Anything above 50 implies growth, but in this case very slight.

The data raised the pressure on the Polish central bank to ease its policy, economists said, as Poland has one of the highest real interest rates in the region and is facing the risk of deflation.

Poland's monetary stance is in contrast with the Czech Republic, which has slashed rates to almost zero and is intervening to weaken the crown.

The Czech Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) dropped to 54.7 in June from a 3-year high hit last month. The slowdown followed a decline in PMI in Germany, the region's main trade partner.

But the Czech data was still firmly in growth territory, aided by a central bank policy of weakening the crown currency, which has helped exporters.

The Polish PMI data came after a disappointing retail sales and industrial output reading last month, signalling that economic growth was likely to slow compared with the first quarter, when the economy expanded by 3.4 percent annually.

"June survey data from HSBC signalled a broad stagnation in Polish manufacturing business conditions," Markit said.

"As for the H2 2014/2015 outlook, improving labour market, strong investment performance in Q1 2014, recovering credit still suggest that the current weakness should not extend," said HSBC CEE economist Agata Urbanska-Giner.

Hungary, which uses a different methodology for its PMI index, reported the index dropped to 51.5 in June from a revised 53.8 in May and was below the average of the past three years.

CONTRAST

The decline in the Czech PMI was mostly driven by external factors, said HSBC's Urbanska-Giner.

"This correction is in line with the German PMI's slide from the beginning of the year," she said. "Industrial production growth is still likely to be climbing higher in the near term."

The Czech index remained in growth for the 14th successive month.

After exiting a record year-and-a-half recession last year, the export-reliant Czech economy's recovery has gathered pace in the past two quarters, lifted by better trade with euro zone partners and improving domestic demand.

Revised data from the statistics office on Tuesday showed the economy grew faster than previously thought in the first quarter, expanding by 0.8 percent on a quarterly basis and by 2.9 percent on an annual basis, the fast since early 2011.

The central bank intervened to weaken the crown in November to fight deflation risks, helping boost exports and retail sales as shoppers stopped waiting for falling prices.

Poland's central bank has, in contrast, been reluctant to cut rates, still remembering years of stubbornly high inflation and afraid that strong economic growth would at some point trigger a rise in consumer prices.

Inflation normally accelerates in tandem with economic growth, but in Poland that link has been broken because credit has been slow, the government is reducing public debt and low inflation in the euro zone, Poland's biggest trade partner, has had a knock-on effect.

Poland's inflation stands at 0.2 percent in annual terms, deep below the central bank target of 2.5 percent.

"Our base-case scenario envisages a stabilisation of rates until year-end, but we note that the risk of a downward move in rates is increasing," Antoniak said, adding that the data also points to a slowdown in second-quarter GDP growth.

Poland's central bank starts its 2-day meeting on rates on Tuesday and will deliver its decision on Wednesday. All but one economists polled by Reuters last week expect the bank to keep its main rate at 2.5 percent. title: Czech c.bank chief says  FX interventions  may continue into 2015
text:
PLZEN, Czech Republic, April 9 (Reuters) - The Czech central bank's foreign exchange intervention regime, aimed at preventing the crown from strengthening, could stay in place past the beginning of 2015, longer than it has signalled so far, Governor Miroslav Singer said on Wednesday.

The bank has said that it would keep its commitment to intervene "at least" until the beginning of 2015, or next year's first monetary meeting due in February, but Singer said soft inflation data may prolong it.

"I would say that this further strengthens the belief that it is necessary to take the word 'at least' very seriously. It is possible that the period will last somewhat longer than until the beginning of the next year," Singer said at a roundtable with business representatives in Plzen, southwest of Prague.

(Reporting by Robert Muller, writing by Jan Lopatka; Editing by John Stonestreet)

    * Polish, Czech central banks meeting this week
    * Telefonica CR shares fall after PPF deal
    By Marton Dunai and Jason Hovet
    BUDAPEST/PRAGUE, Nov 5 (Reuters) - The leu fell a touch on
Tuesday when the Romanian central bank cut interest rates to a
new record low, the first in a series rate setting meetings in
central Europe this week.
    With rates across the region falling to record lows in the
past year, borrowing costs have likely reached or are near
bottom as economies look to re-gain some traction after slowing
in the wake of the euro zone crisis.
    The space for Romania's central bank to cut interest rates
has narrowed but the bank could still use other tools to ease
monetary policy, Governor Mugur Isarescu said on Tuesday.
    Markets will also look to a rate decision on Wednesday in
Poland, where rates are unlikely to go any lower, and on
Thursday in the Czech Republic, where the threat of currencyintervention as a tool to ease policy is weighing on the crown.
    In the Czech Republic, data on Tuesday showed retail sales
rose by an annual 3.7 percent in September, in line with
forecasts. 
    BNP Paribas analysts said a recovery in consumption reduced
the chance of interventions by the central bank (CNB) to weaken
the crown. "The CNB is unlikely to initiate interventions," BNP
said. "This is the main premise for trading the CZK markets."
    By 1413 GMT, the crown had dipped less than 0.1
percent to 25.827 to the euro, just off an October low, and the
leu was down 0.1 percent at 4.439.

loans.

title: POLL-Czech  central bank  to avoid crown  intervention  for now
text:
PRAGUE, Sept 23 (Reuters) - The Czech central bank won't opt to intervene against the crown currency when it meets on Thursday but the possibility is not likely to disappear in the coming months, according to a Reuters poll.

With the Czech key two-week repo rate at 0.05 percent since November, the bank has been considering weakening the crown as a policy tool to aid recovery in an economy just getting out of a record recession.

Fifteen of 18 analysts polled by Reuters between Sept. 16-23 expect rate setters to opt against intervention this month. Three analysts did not answer.

While the Czech economy has just emerged from its longest-ever period of contraction, analysts say low inflation and a currency that has stayed resilient to a selloff in emerging markets since the summer will keep the threat of intervention alive.

"Although CPI growth fell further in the Czech Republic, expected recovery in the euro zone should ease the pressure to launch intervention," said Tomas Holinka, analyst with Moody's Analytics.

The central bank (CNB) formally voted on interventions at its last meeting in August but decided against stepping into the market, which would be its first such move in over a decade.

The bank will release new economic forecasts in November.

"We think that the hawks are likely still in a mild majority. Hence, the new November forecast likely has to persuade them," Jaromir Sindel, Citibank's chief economist in Prague, said.

As trade with the euro zone faltered and consumers held back spending while facing job uncertainty, central Europe's policymakers have slashed interest rates in the past year.

Intervention would help prop up price growth by making imports more expensive, enticing people to spend now. A weaker crown would also help exporters, raising their income and bringing more money into the economy.

But it carries risks and could even backfire by depressing consumer demand. (Reporting by Mirka Krufova and Jason Hovet; Editing by Ruth Pitchford)

title: CEE Morning Briefing: Region Watching Fed, Polish Minutes Due
text:
TODAY'S CALENDAR 
Local/GMT 
1130/0930 Hungary government bond auction 
1400/1200 Polish minutes from Sept rate meeting 
 

Central European markets Thursday morning will have their first chance to react to decision of the U.S. Federal Reserve's policy meeting, which surprised markets on Wednesday.

The Federal Open Market Committee said in its post-meeting policy-setting statement that it would continue to buy $85 billion in bonds each month. Investors had expected the central bank to pare its bond-buying programs by between $10 billion and $15 billion at this meeting.

"It's amazing, and certainly not what we thought would happen," said Marc Doss, a San Diego, Calif.-based regional chief investment officer with Wells Fargo Private Bank. "We were definitely in the camp they would do $10 to $15 billion" less purchasing each month.

Elsewhere in the region, the Polish central bank will publish minutes from its September monetary policy meeting when it left rates unchanged.

Poland's monetary policy council cut the benchmark rate to an all-time low of 2.5% in an easing campaign between November and July as inflation and growth slowed hand in hand. In August inflation reached 1.1% on year, significantly below the central bank's 2.5% goal.

Comments from monetary policy council members recently are centered on the message that interest rates will remain on hold at least until end-2013.

In Budapest, Hungary will offer a total of 44 billion forints ($197 million) worth of three-year, five-year and 15-year bonds at an auction Thursday. The series on offer are reopened issues.

The agency last auctioned the three- and five-year bonds on Sept. 5, while the 15-year bond was last reopened in April.

title: WSJ Blog:Czech  Central Bank  on the Fence about  FX Intervention
text:
(This story has been posted on The Wall Street Journal Online's Emerging Europe blog at http://blogs.wsj.com/emergingeurope/)

By Sean Carney

The longest-ever Czech recession continues unabated as fresh data Monday showed export growth weakening and industrial output contracting, but still hasn't tipped the balance of opinion towards central bank intervention to weaken the koruna.

"The monetary policy board has seven members and only three members want immediate action. It's going to be difficult to convince the fourth. Interventions are costly for the bank and the outlook is very uncertain, " said economist Vladimír Pikora at Nextfinance in Prague.

The indicators Monday showed that imports and exports are falling even though the country enjoys a foreign trade surplus, suggesting that domestic and foreign demand are weak.

This comes as inflation decreased 0.4 percentage point to 1.3% in May from April, well below the central bank's 2% target.

The central bank, which last year cut its benchmark interest rate to 0.05%, believes that overall risks to the economy are disinflationary and "tilted to a need for easier monetary conditions," according to minutes from the central bank's June 27 policy meeting, also released Monday.

The central bank said the data strengthen the disinflationary trend that it noted six weeks ago.

"The board members also agreed that the need to further ease the monetary conditions had increased compared to the situation" in mid-May, the minutes said.

But launching an intervention is still a hotly contested topic on the seven-member monetary policy board.

"Several board members spoke in favor of immediately commencing foreign exchange interventions. However, it was also said that the tendency to undershoot the inflation target was only short term in nature and that a necessary condition for commencing interventions was a risk of sustained deflation, which was not materialising," the minutes said.

Elements that make a potential intervention more likely include the Czech Republic's current political uncertainty, which may prevent fiscal policy from easing as was expected, so "monetary policy would have to take this into account" the central bank said.

It said the scope of potential interventions was "unlimited," adding that a weaker koruna would impact the economy more quickly than interest rate changes.

There are several factors working against an intervention, namely the koruna is trading against the euro at a weaker level than the central bank forecasts.

"It's entirely possible that the remainder of the [monetary policy] board is quietly betting that euro-zone developments will work on behalf of the Czech central bank and market developments themselves will weaken the koruna," Nextfinance's Mr. Pikora said.

Additionally, the tendency to undershoot the inflation target "was only short term in nature and that a necessary condition for commencing interventions was a risk of sustained deflation, which was not materialising," the minutes said.

The central bank also noted that the current improvement in German consumer confidence offered hope that a turnaround in external demand for Czech goods might materialise.

Citfin analyst Jiri Simek said Monday's economic indicators aren't great but can be seen as part of a larger picture over which local monetary policy has little influence.

Industrial output declined in May largely due to the country's mining sector posting an annual production decrease of more than 25% in the month, but that was mainly because of record-low coal prices.

An annual decline in automobile sales in May followed a surge the previous month.

"I wouldn't view these numbers so tragically. For the whole year, industrial output growth should be about zero, it's not going to have a major impact on the economy," Mr. Simek said.

title: DJ Monetary Easing to Continue in Central Europe Next Week
text:
PRAGUE--Further monetary easing is likely in Central Europe next week with an expected lowering of interest rates in Poland, following a cut in Hungary and dovish talk of foreign exchange interventions in the Czech Republic.

In Warsaw, Poland's central bank is expected to cut its benchmark interest rates 0.25 percentage point to a new all-time low of 2.5%, all 18 analysts polled by Dow Jones Newswires said.

The aim is to help the slowing economy regain momentum and to bring slowing inflation closer to the central bank's target of 2.5%, which is the midpoint in the wider 1.5% to 3.5% tolerance range.

The rate council has lowered borrowing costs by two percentage points since November 2012 as the economy nearly stagnated in the first quarter with annual growth of 0.5%, while inflation eased to 0.5% in May.

Originally some market participants saw a risk of a deeper interest rate cut but the recently weakening zloty has shifted expectations.

Since the rate council's early June meeting the zloty has weakened from 4.25 against the euro to 4.32 midday Friday.

"If you asked me a few weeks ago I would have said there is a risk of a 0.5 percentage point rate cut," Raiffeisen Bank economist Marta Petka-Zagajewska said. "However, with the zloty where it is I see a risk there will be no cut at all."

The cut in Poland would follow a similar move in Hungary, where the central bank cut the policy rate 25 basis points to 4.25% on June 25 amid an easing cycle that began in August 2012 in a bid to liven up its lackluster economy.

And would come as the Czech central bank, which has its benchmark rate at the historic low of 0.05%, on Thursday said the likelihood of launching an intervention to weaken the koruna is increasing as it foresees "no tangible inflationary risks."

As it has no more room to lower interest rates, the next available tool is the exchange rate.

"Risks to [the economy] are generally disinflationary; they are pointing towards the need for looser monetary conditions than is expected in [the bank's] forecasts," the central bank said without adding when a move may come.

In Prague, households are slowing returning to shops and spending, but the annual increase in retail sales posted in April is likely to be offset by a minor decrease in May.

The data will follow the early-Friday release of revised Czech gross domestic product data that showed household consumption contracted by a mild 0.5% annually in the first quarter and it actually increased by 1.7% on a quarterly basis in the period.

Households are spending more in step with the government increasing its spending by 1.2% on year and 1% on a quarterly basis in the first three months of this year.

title: CEE MARKETS- Currencies , stocks fall on Fed and economy worries
text:
BUCHAREST, May 23 (Reuters) - Hungary's forint led emerging European currencies lower on Thursday after hawkish comments by U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke knocked riskier assets around the world.

Central European assets, offering better returns than more developed markets because of their higher degree of risk, have benefited from a wall of cheap money created by central bank stimulus. However, they often suffer more when global sentiment sours.

Stocks fell across the region, led by a 1.3 percent drop in Warsaw, after Bernanke's remarks sparked worries of an earlier than expected reduction in U.S. monetary stimulus, while weak Chinese economic data added to worries.

"The weakening is due to the Fed, what Bernanke said, which triggered a rise in risk aversion and we are affected the most," a Budapest dealer said. "Everything is weakening but we weaken more as the forint had firmed the most before."

The forint, which had gained 5 percent in the last month, fell 0.6 percent to 290.75 per euro by 0741 GMT, and was followed by Poland's zloty, which dropped 0.4 percent.

Expectations of lower interest rates are also keeping some pressure on currencies. Hungary's central bank is expected to cut next week and more easing is also seen in Poland.

Rates are close to zero in the Czech Republic and the central bank has threatened to intervene to weaken the crown to help a recession-hit economy. The currency was 0.1 percent higher on the day and analysts said pressure would persist given the possibility of central bank action.

In Romania, where the central bank has also flagged a rate cutting cycle ahead, the leu lost 0.2 percent to 4.357 per euro, continuing a retreat from a 16-month high hit early in May.

The finance ministry may also struggle to sell 10-year debt at a tender later in the day, given yields on the secondary market rose about 15 basis points from Wednesday, and analysts and dealers said longer-term the currency could continue to fall towards 4.40.

"The whole market was looking for a reason to sell, so the 


region is under pressure," said a Bucharest dealer.

title: UPDATE 1-Czech  central bank  hits crown with  intervention  comment
text:
* Bank debating interventions "quite often", says governor Singer

* Crown eases to one-week low

* Says commercial banks' profitability is falling

(Adds details, comment)

PRAGUE, May 7 (Reuters) - The Czech central bank often discusses intervening to weaken the crown, its governor said, in comments that hit the currency.

In a presentation at an economic conference on Tuesday, Singer also said Czech lenders were facing increased pressure to cut margins and their profits may fall in coming years.

The central bank cut the key two-week repo rate to 0.05 percent in November and said that, if it needed to ease policy further, it would use interventions to weaken the crown.

Inflation is falling in the Czech Republic, which has been locked in a recession since mid-2011.

"We are discussing interventions quite often now," Singer said. The crown eased to a one-week low of 25.80 to the euro

after the comment, from 25.748 earlier, according to Reuters data.

The currency has been on a downward path since the rate cut, falling to a 17-month low in April and removing the need for the central bank to step into the market.

A weaker currency makes imports more expensive, raising inflation which has dropped below the bank's 2 percent target. It would also raise exporters' revenues.

Some central bankers have however warned that a weaker crown would further crimp household demand, suppressed by three years of austerity measures.

BANKS UNDER PRESSURE

Czechs' thrift has also hit lending, causing loan growth to households to slow, Singer said, and consumer loans have been shrinking since 2011.

That has hit banks whose margins are also under pressure from the record low interest rates.

Lender Komercni Banka said on Tuesday net profit fell by almost 10 percent in the first quarter, citing falling interest margins and fees.

"We think that (banks) will not be able to create such (big) profits as they did in the past, which does not mean that they will not be able to create very decent profits in the European context," Singer said.

title: CEE MARKETS 2-Hungarian bonds retreat, CEE  currencies  mixed
text:
* Investors switch into Hungary's fx bonds

* Currencies mixed, flow into Romanian bonds lifts leu

* Attention turning to Czech central bank meeting

By Jason Hovet and Sandor Peto

PRAGUE/BUDAPEST, April 26 (Reuters) - Forint-denominated Hungarian government bonds retreated on Friday as investors continued to shift into foreign currency debt following a decline in domestic yields.

Investors globally are seeking higher yields offered by emerging market assets relative to developed markets. In Romania, domestic debt as well as foreign currency debt is in demand, due to still high yields, and demand for Romanian paper on Friday lifted the leu.

Central European policymakers have been cutting interest rates to help their economies fight recession or economic slowdown, but yields are still mostly attractive.

Hungary's central bank has cut its base rate nine times, each by a quarter percentage point, since August to 4.75 percent.

Markets have priced in further cuts to 3.50 percent, pushing yields on forint-denominated bonds to record lows in the past few weeks and below yields on euro- and dollar-denominated bonds. Foreign currency bond yields would normally be lower as forint bonds usually include a yield premium to cover foreign investors' exchange rate risk.

"Many local funds have now switched to foreign currency bonds (in the past few days), and in linked derivatives deals investors can get an additional yield premium," a Budapest-based fixed income trader said.

"The yields on 10-year dollar bonds have come down (in recent days) to near 5 percent from 5.5, while the 10-year forint bond yield rose to 5.45 percent from 5.3 percent," the trader said.

In the Czech Republic, where the central bank has already cut rates to near zero, the yield on 10-year eurobonds

fell to record lows below 2 percent.

Currencies in the region were mixed, with the Czech crown

firming 0.2 percent and the Romanian leu gaining 0.1 percent against the euro by 1444 GMT. The forint

eased 0.4 percent and the Polish zloty shed 0.2 percent.

Weak data from the region and from main trading partner Germany, along with cuts in interest rates, have weighed on the regions' currencies in the past few months.

Romania, though, has resisted cutting rates to boost its slumping economy because of nagging concerns over inflation, and strong demand for the country's bonds after they were included in regional indices has underpinned its currency.

"It seems like another day of gains for the leu, and central bank agents don't seem to be on the bid side noticeably," said a dealer in Bucharest. "The main support is still the longer-term trend of flows into bonds."

Yields on Romanian 10-year bonds fell 58 basis points at an auction on Thursday, boosting the leu.

In Czech markets, attention was turning to a central bank meeting next week.

Analysts in a Reuters poll on Thursday said the crown's losses over recent weeks had eliminated the chance of the central bank stepping in to weaken the currency for now as a way of easing monetary conditions.

With interest rates already at 0.05 percent, the bank has been toying with the idea of intervention in its battle with the Czech Republic's longest recession in two decades.

The crown touched its lowest since November 2011 this week.

title: Czech c.banker says  interventions  not required -Bloomberg
text:
PRAGUE, April 24 (Reuters) - The Czech Republic does not face a deflation threat that would require currency interventions to ease monetary policy further, Czech central bank board member Pavel Rezabek was quoted as saying on Wednesday.

The central bank cut interest rates to near zero last year and said it would step into markets to weaken the crown against the euro if it needs to ease further.

Rezabek said in an interview with Bloomberg that the primary goal of interventions, if conducted, would be to "solve a deflation problem".

"The risk of deflation has significantly declined, and we can say it may have even been fully eliminated, unless a major shock occurs," Rezabek was quoted as saying. "We should be careful about using this instrument as long as inflation on the policy horizon isn't at risk."

title: UPDATE 1-Czech c.bank minutes: risks to economic forecast point to easier policy
text:
(Adds background, details)

PRAGUE, April 5 (Reuters) - A majority of Czech central bank policymakers agreed that risks to the bank's economic forecast pointed to the need for lightly looser policy, minutes of their March meeting showed, highlighting the likelihood the bank could intervene to weaken the crown.

With the key two-week repo rate at 0.05 percent, a level the central bank calls "a technical zero", policymakers have said they would not cut it any more and would use FX interventions if there is a need to relax policy further.

Central bank Governor Miroslav Singer said after the March 28 meeting that risks were skewed to the downside, which would indicate a need for loosening. However, the crown has weakened since then, partly due to the Cyprus crisis, dampening the need for intervention.

The Czech Republic is mired in its longest recession in two decades, worsened by a budget squeeze by the centre-right government which has hit consumption and prompted the central bank to cut interest rates to near zero.

The point was raised at the March 28 policy meeting that domestic economic activity was more subdued than forecast and was anti-inflationary, the minutes of showed on Friday.

The economy shrank for a fourth straight quarter in the final three months of 2012 and by more than the central bank forecast, while inflation stood at 1.7 percent in February, below the bank's outlook for 2.0 percent, which is also its target rate.

Policymakers pointed out repeatedly at the March meeting that directly influencing the exchange rate was an effective instrument in a small and open economy where policy rates are at zero.

However, the minutes showed that opinion among the seven members of the governing board was split on the effect of potential interventions.

Some argued that any interventions to weaken the crown would raise prices of imported goods, which would prompt people to spend now rather than put off purchases on expectations prices would fall.

But it was also argued that a weaker crown would raise prices of "less elastic" items in the consumer basket such as food and energy, which might conversely depress aggregate consumption.

title: CEE MORNING BRIEFING: Hungary's Budgetary Outlook, EU Tax Eyed
text:
TODAY'S CALENDAR 
Local/GMT 
1030/0930 Czech central banker Hampl at conference on EU tax 
1030/0930 Hungary PM speaks at Bruegel Institute 
1130/1030 Hungary auctions 12-month T-bill 
1545/1445 Hungary PM Orban, EC President Barroso briefing 
 

Hungary's budgetary outlook will be under scrutiny in Brussels on Wednesday, while a Czech central banker will speak on a European Union proposal to directly tax the bloc's citizens.

Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban will meet European Commission President Jose Manuel Barroso in Brussels on Wednesday to talk about the country's budget and whether the EC will allow Hungary to exit the Excessive Deficit Procedure.

The EDP, which Hungary has been under since joining the European Union in 2004, acts as fiscal-restraint mechanism on countries that fail to reduce their budget deficits to below the EU's ceiling of 3% of gross domestic product.

As Hungary's economy has been shrinking due to falling investment and domestic consumption over the past two years, Mr. Orban's government has been reliant on widely criticized taxes on international companies that harm business confidence, growth and employment in the medium and longer term, analysts say.

The Commission said Monday that rather than seek revenues via controversial taxes, Mr. Orban's government should instead cut spending.

In Prague, Mojmir Hampl, the Czech central bank's vice governor and an outspoken euro-skeptic, will speak on EU proposals for a pan-EU tax, that would likely be incorporated into existing value-added taxes, in theory giving the bloc its own revenue stream free of reliance on contributions from national governments.

The idea is part of a two-pronged attempt by Brussels to raise revenue for the bloc, the other element being a tax on financial transactions.

Mr. Hampl may also comment on the outlook for monetary easing in the Czech Republic via intervention on foreign exchange markets. The central bank exhausted its standard monetary-policy toolbox last autumn when it cut its benchmark interest rate to 0.05%.

POLAND: Italian bank UniCredit SpA (UCG.MI) Tuesday launched the sale of up to 9.1% of its Polish subsidiary Bank Pekao SA to institutional investors through an accelerated bookbuilding.

POLAND: Polish economic growth slowed significantly last year, data showed on Tuesday, raising fears that the economy could soon be on the verge of contracting for the first time in more than two decades.

A downturn would be a tough blow for Poland, which until recently had stood up well against fallout from the debt crisis afflicting the neighboring euro zone, its largest trading partner.

CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech Prime Minister Petr Necas Tuesday dismissed renewed calls by his junior coalition partners to adopt the European Union's fiscal compact and subject Czech budgetary policies to EU oversight.

Mr. Necas instead proposed that the Czech government draft its own fiscal responsibility rules, including setting limits on the level of the national debt. The new rules would require a constitutional amendment, Mr. Necas said in a statement.

HUNGARY: Hungary's Development Ministry is preparing further utility tariff cuts that would reduce water, sewage, communal waste collection, and chimney inspection fees, a government official told state news agency MTI Tuesday.

The government discussed the possibility of the price cuts at its Tuesday meeting as well as the results of the 10% price cut in retail electricity prices that came in to affect on Jan. 1, state secretary Janos Fonagy told the news agency.

HUNGARY: Hungary's rate setters regard their current monetary policy tool set as adequate to maneuver, the rate setters said Tuesday in response to recent comments from the government that the central bank should help it boost growth with unconventional monetary policy measures.

"The Monetary Policy Council was fully unanimous with regard to this issue," Andras Simor, governor of the National Bank of Hungary, said at a press conference after the central bank cut rates as expected by financial markets.

ROMANIA: Peruvian President Ollanta Humala met with his Romanian counterpart, Traian Basescu, on Tuesday to discuss several areas where the countries could increase cooperation.

During a statement following the meeting, the presidents said they discussed increasing ties in the areas of education, health care, technology, and trade. "We have a lot of potential [to increase trade]," Mr. Humala said. "Our economies are complementary."

BULGARIA: A referendum in Bulgaria on whether to build a second nuclear power plant has failed due to insufficient turnout, official results showed Tuesday. Only 1.4 million people, or just over 20% of the electorate, voted in Sunday's poll, far short of the 60% needed for the plebiscite to be valid, electoral officials said.

Hungary's budgetary outlook will be under scrutiny in Brussels on Wednesday, while a Czech central banker will speak on a European Union proposal to directly tax the bloc's citizens.

Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban will meet European Commission President Jose Manuel Barroso in Brussels on Wednesday to talk about the country's budget and whether the EC will allow Hungary to exit the Excessive Deficit Procedure.

The EDP, which Hungary has been under since joining the European Union in 2004, acts as fiscal-restraint mechanism on countries that fail to reduce their budget deficits to below the EU's ceiling of 3% of gross domestic product.

As Hungary's economy has been shrinking due to falling investment and domestic consumption over the past two years, Mr. Orban's government has been reliant on widely criticized taxes on international companies that harm business confidence, growth and employment in the medium and longer term, analysts say.

The Commission said Monday that rather than seek revenues via controversial taxes, Mr. Orban's government should instead cut spending.

In Prague, Mojmir Hampl, the Czech central bank's vice governor and an outspoken euro-skeptic, will speak on EU proposals for a pan-EU tax, that would likely be incorporated into existing value-added taxes, in theory giving the bloc its own revenue stream free of reliance on contributions from national governments.

The idea is part of a two-pronged attempt by Brussels to raise revenue for the bloc, the other element being a tax on financial transactions.

Mr. Hampl may also comment on the outlook for monetary easing in the Czech Republic via intervention on foreign exchange markets. The central bank exhausted its standard monetary-policy toolbox last autumn when it cut its benchmark interest rate to 0.05%.

title: CEE MARKETS 2- Currencies  and stocks slip, leu close to high
text:
* Prospect of U.S. fiscal crunch pressures assets

* Romanian leu, stocks still close to highs after election

By Jason Hovet and Sam Cage

PRAGUE/BUCHAREST, Dec 28 (Reuters) - C entral European currencies a nd stocks were a touch lower on Friday as U.S. lawmakers sought to avoid an end of year f iscal crunch, while Rom ania's leu a n d stocks rem ained close to sev en-month highs due to increased political stability.

Stock markets in central Europe fell up to 0.5 percent - though the Warsaw bourse was close to its highest since mid-2011.

Bonds were flat, with Polish yields close to record lows after Warsaw said it planned to have more than half its 2013 financing needs covered after the first quarter.

Investors were eyeing last-minute efforts by U.S. officials to reach a deal that would avoid some $600 billion in tax hikes and spending cuts due to kick in at the end of the year.

Few analysts predict a deal that will deal with all the issues dividing Republicans and Democrats at once but many have tempered concern by speculating the government will muddle through and find deals that can ease some of the worst of the impact on the economy.

"In general, the market seems to be positive and expectant with regards to the U.S. solution, though (market) volatility is likely to prevail until the very last moment," a dealer in Budapest said.

The R omania n leu is the region's worst-performing currency i n a year which has seen it flick between f our governments, preventing th e central bank from following its peers and cutting rates to support growth.

The leu slipped 0.2 percent to 4.435 per euro by 1251 GMT , b ut remained c lose to a seven-month high hit after a new government took office following a convincing election win. The Bucharest bourse hit its highest since May. [ID: nL5E8NL3KG]

"We see the RON caught in the 4.42-4.44 per euro range for this year's last couple of sessions," said ING analyst Mihai Tantaru.

COOLING MARKET

The forint and zloty have led gains in emerging Europe this year with r ises of 8.1 percent and 9.5 percent respectively, as their higher yields attracted investors in a rally fuelled by major global central banks' liquidity-boosting measures.

Easing monetary policy in the region has cooled the market in the last half of 2012, though, causing currencies to mostly flatten out going into 2013.

The Hungarian forint dropped to its lowest level versus the euro since June this week while the local market was closed for a holiday, but it has regained about half those losses.

T he forint inched up 0. 2 percent to 29 0.8 to the euro, after reaching a low of 295.5 on Wednesday. P oland's zloty

was down 0. 3 percent a t 4.079 .

In the Czech Republic, the central bank has said currency interventions to weaken the crown could be the next monetary easing tool now that rates are near zero. Dealers have said the level of 25 to the euro could be decisive for the bank.

The currency, which has gained nearly 2 percent this year, w as 0 .3 percent lower at 25.119 t o the euro.

"There is not much power to push the crown below 25," a Prague currency dealer said.

title: CNB-Czech Central Banker Lizal Sees No Inflationary Pressures
text:
Release date - 10122012

Czech foreign-exchange intervention to weaken the koruna may come in mid-2013 and the central bank’s near-zero interest rates may remain until late 2014 as no inflationary pressures can be seen, a central banker said Monday.

In an interview, Lubomir Lizal, a member of the bank’s monetary policy board, said the central bank’s record-low benchmark interest rate of 0.05% will remain in place until inflationary pressures emerge.

When asked if he sees any inflationary risks at present, he simply said ‘no.’

When asked how long rates can remain near zero, he said ‘I’d rather target conditions and not periods of time.’

In the central bank’s own forecasts, which span a period of 18 months, there are no indications of any rising pressures on consumer prices, he said.

The country’s headline inflation rate was above the central bank’s 1% to 3% target range in the first 10 months of the year, but that was largely due to increases in value-added taxes that took effect in January.

Monetary policy-relevant inflation, which looks at prices that can be influenced by monetary policy, has been in the lower end of the target inflation range all year, taking pressure off rate-setters.

The Czech economy has been in recession since late 2011, as domestic demand tumbled amid falling real wages, tax hike-fueled inflation, rising unemployment, government spending cuts and negative fallout from the euro zone’s many crises.

As a result the central bank has largely exhausted its standard monetary toolbox centered on interest rates and now is considering how to further ease monetary conditions if the need should arise.

Mr. Lizal said that now that interest rates are close to zero, ‘the natural question is what’s next. For a small, open economy like the Czech Republic, in current conditions foreign exchange (intervention) is the best second tool you have.’

The central bank is not considering other non-standard monetary tools such as quantitative easing, as the Czech financial system already enjoys a surplus of liquidity and putting more money into the system would not help.

Mr. Lizal said he doesn’t favor a particular foreign exchange rate for the koruna, but rather will gauge policy needs via inflation, economic performance and current market developments.

‘Based on the latest prognosis from the central bank, it suggests further monetary easing in the middle of next year,’ Mr. Lizal said, adding that the bank’s forecasts have been largely accurate in the recent past and so he is comfortable with this estimation.

The discussion now is about the tool to use, not how and when to use it, he said without directly responding to a question on what foreign exchange rate he’d like to see.

On Oct. 19, Kamil Janacek, Mr. Lizal’s peer on the central bank’s seven-strong monetary policy board, said an exchange rate of above 25 koruna to the euro is good for exporters and the economy and is the strongest foreign exchange rate he’d like to see so long as the economy is weak.

At 1402 GMT Monday, the koruna traded at 25.25 to the euro. The koruna has remained above 25 to the euro since late October.

Mr. Lizal also said any recovery by the Czech export-based economy hinges on a return to growth in the euro zone, which is the Czech Republic’s largest trading partner.

title: *DJ Czech Central Banker Lizal Sees No Inflationary Pressures
text:
10 Dec 2012 09:58 EDT *DJ  Czech Lizal: Next Monetary Easing Likely Mid-2013

10 Dec 2012 09:58 EDT *DJ  Czech Lizal: FX Intervention Next Tool For Monetary Easing

10 Dec 2012 09:59 EDT *DJ  Czech Lizal: Near-Zero Rates Possible Into 2H 2014

10 Dec 2012 09:59 EDT *DJ  Czech Lizal: Quantitative Easing Makes No Sense for Czech Econ

10 Dec 2012 10:04 EDT DJ  Czech Central Banker Lizal Sees No Inflationary Pressures

By Sean Carney

PRAGUE--Czech foreign-exchange intervention to weaken the koruna may come in mid-2013 and the central bank's near-zero interest rates may remain until late 2014 as no inflationary pressures can be seen, a central banker said Monday.

In an interview, Lubomir Lizal, a member of the bank's monetary policy board, said the central bank's record-low benchmark interest rate of 0.05% will remain in place until inflationary pressures emerge.

When asked if he sees any inflationary risks at present, he simply said "no."

When asked how long rates can remain near zero, he said "I'd rather target conditions and not periods of time."

In the central bank's own forecasts, which span a period of 18 months, there are no indications of any rising pressures on consumer prices, he said.

The country's headline inflation rate was above the central bank's 1% to 3% target range in the first 10 months of the year, but that was largely due to increases in value-added taxes that took effect in January.

Monetary policy-relevant inflation, which looks at prices that can be influenced by monetary policy, has been in the lower end of the target inflation range all year, taking pressure off rate-setters.

The Czech economy has been in recession since late 2011, as domestic demand tumbled amid falling real wages, tax hike-fueled inflation, rising unemployment, government spending cuts and negative fallout from the euro zone's many crises.

As a result the central bank has largely exhausted its standard monetary toolbox centered on interest rates and now is considering how to further ease monetary conditions if the need should arise.

Mr. Lizal said that now that interest rates are close to zero, "the natural question is what's next. For a small, open economy like the Czech Republic, in current conditions foreign exchange (intervention) is the best second tool you have."

The central bank isn't considering other non-standard monetary tools such as quantitative easing, as the Czech financial system already enjoys a surplus of liquidity and putting more money into the system wouldn't help.

Mr. Lizal said he doesn't favor a particular foreign exchange rate for the koruna, but rather will gauge policy needs via inflation, economic performance and current market developments.

"Based on the latest prognosis from the central bank, it suggests further monetary easing in the middle of next year," Mr. Lizal said, adding that the bank's forecasts have been largely accurate in the recent past and so he is comfortable with this estimation.

The discussion now is about the tool to use, not how and when to use it, he said without directly responding to a question on what foreign exchange rate he'd like to see.

On Oct. 19, Kamil Janacek, Mr. Lizal's peer on the central bank's seven-strong monetary policy board, said an exchange rate of above 25 koruna ($0.11) to the euro is good for exporters and the economy and is the strongest foreign exchange rate he'd like to see so long as the economy is weak.

At 1402 GMT Monday, the koruna traded at 25.25 to the euro. The koruna has remained above 25 to the euro since late October.

Mr. Lizal also said any recovery by the Czech export-based economy hinges on a return to growth in the euro zone, which is the Czech Republic's largest trading partner.

title: UPDATE 1-Czech c.banker: no need for QE,  interventions  possible
text:
(Adds quote, background)

PRAGUE, Nov 20 (Reuters) - The Czech Republic does not need quantitative easing but that does not stop the central bank from considering market interventions to weaken the crown, the bank's Vice-Governor Mojmir Hampl said on Tuesday.

The bank has said interventions would be the next tool if it needs to relax policy further after cutting its main repo rate to 0.05 percent this month.

Governor Miroslav Singer has said there may be a need to ease policy more around the middle of 2013.

"When my colleague Singer says something about possible entry into the foreign exchange market, let me remind you that this is not a thought about this market, this economy needing some liquidity injections," Hampl told an economic seminar.

"This is in a situation when you cannot go below zero in interest rates and you have the feeling that there are anti-inflationary risks, you will not meet the inflation target, then one of the first tools that comes into mind is the exchange rate, with all the risks that it entails."

Hampl's six-year term runs out in December but he may be reappointed for another one.

He has repeatedly spoken against non-standard policies, such as the quantitative easing employed in the United States and Britain to pump money into the economy, saying the economy was fundamentally sound and did not need it.

An intervention to weaken the crown would increase the local value of exporters' earnings. Price rises caused by a weaker exchange rate would also help the bank bring inflation up towards its 2 percent target.

The crown traded at 25.270 to the euro on Tuesday. It has lost 3.4 percent since Singer began talking about interventions or other easing tools, compared to a 0.9 percent weakening of the Polish zloty and the Romanian leu

and a 0.4 percent firming of the Hungarian forint

in the same period.

15 Nov 2012 08:10 EDT *DJ  Czech Central Banker: Looser Monetary Policy Needed through Mid-2013

15 Nov 2012 08:49 EDT DJ  Czech Central Banker: Forex Intervention Key Policy Tool

By Leos Rousek

TRUTNOV, Czech Republic--The Czech National Bank will focus on using foreign exchange market intervention to keep the koruna weak, as the outlook for Czech exports remains poor due to recession in the euro area, the central bank governor said Thursday.

"The foreign exchange market remains our key policy channel," Miroslav Singer told the annual conference of the country's Exporters' Association held in Trutnov, north-east of Prague.

Two weeks ago the CNB lowered its headline interest to 0.05% and said that after bringing the rate to nearly zero it may use the exchange rate as its main policy tool. By weakening the koruna Czech goods and services may be priced more cheaply on foreign markets and help local exporters.

"Price pressures remain tame, which warrants looser monetary policies," Mr. Singer said. "The looser policy may be needed until about the middle of the next year."

Mr. Singer declined to specify an adequate exchange rate of the Czech currency against the euro. However, he described the current koruna levels at above 25.00 against the euro as weak.

Czech exporters will continue to face strong head winds at least through the rest of the year, Mr. Singer said.

The Czech economy contracted 0.3% in the three months through end-September against the previous quarter, intensifying its recession. The country's gross domestic product has been contracting for five consecutive quarter, the longest economic slump since its previous deep recession in 1996-97.

Declines in consumer spending, weighed by the growing unemployment and declining real disposable incomes, were the main driver of the GDP slide, while easing net exports were no longer able to offset the poor domestic demand.

title: Flight From Risk Thrashes Emerging-Market  Currencies , Debt
text:
-Global economic anxieties pummel emerging-market assets

-Host of central banks suspected of intervening as their currencies tumble

-South Africa, the Czech Republic hold policy rates steady


 
   Cynthia Lin 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Emerging-market assets fell under severe pressure Thursday as fears about the euro-zone credit crisis and global economic slowdown hit a boiling point despite the Federal Reserve's latest stimulus plan.

U.S. central bankers confirmed market expectations Wednesday, announcing that it will implement what most market participants call "Operation Twist," by buying longer-dated Treasurys and selling shorter-dated ones. The central bank's decision did little to allay mounting fears about the sputtering global economy, sparking an exodus out of risky assets and into the refuge of U.S. government debt.

As Treasury yields plummeted, the risk premium investors demand to hold what they perceive as riskier emerging-market debt increased. This spread as reflected on the J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Global, or Embig, was 32 basis points wider to 449 basis points above Treasurys. In price terms, the index lost 1.49%. The Latin America regional sub-index lost 1.69% in price as its spread blew out 34 basis points to 5.14% over Treasurys.

Emerging-market currencies also took a beating across the board as the U.S. dollar soared, led by notable declines in the Mexican peso, Chilean peso and Korean won.

A slew central banks in Asia--including Korea, Taiwan and Thailand--were suspected to have intervened in the foreign exchange markets to lend support to their currencies. The Korean won was a notable underperformer in its region, weakening to KRW1,181.1 a dollar from KRW1,148.6--now the weakest since last September, according to CQG.

In Brazil, the country's central bank announced midday and quickly implemented an auction of $2.7 billion in foreign-exchange swap contracts to rein in the depreciating real. The battered Brazilian currency opened at 1.92 reais to the dollar, weakening sharply to BRL1.94 at one point. On the Embig, Brazil's risk premium increased 29 basis points to 285 basis points, losing 0.97% in price.

Such efforts come in stark contrast to moves these central banks conducted just months ago, when many complained that their currencies were strengthening too quickly and hurting exporters at home. Earlier in the year, these assets showed impressive resilience even when the situation in advanced nations began to crumble. But the rout since the start of September shows that these regions are still inextricably linked to the developed world.

"The emerging-market space is interesting because it held and held and held," said Michael Mata, portfolio manager at ING's global bond fund, "but, in the end, there's no way to decouple from 50% of global GDP." Mata's team believes there's still more room from emerging-market currencies to fall as these nations' policymakers cut rates and reduce the interest-rate differential that made their currencies so appealing.

These days, inflation and other issues that come with red-hot economic growth is taking a back seat, with fears of a double-dip recession and the intensifying euro-zone credit crisis dominating investors' fears. The latest economic reports Thursday show the euro zone's composite purchase manufacturing index falling into the sub-50 contraction territory for the first time since 2009, while China's PMI sank deeper in the contraction range to 49.4 from 49.9.

South Africa's central bank decided to keep its policy rate at 5.5%, caught in a dilemma of slowing growth and rising inflation. The South African rand weakened to ZAR8.2963 a dollar from ZAR8.2530, which Reserve Bank Governor Gill Marcus acknowledged is putting the country's goal of keeping inflation under 6% at risk.

Monetary authorities of the Czech Republic also convened Thursday and decided to keep rates steady a record-low 0.75%. Central and Eastern European currencies have been rattled this month give their ties to the neighboring euro zone.
